segments.text: Thank you. It's time to settle in for our last and very interesting session. Please, those of us who are outside, come in so we can have a wonderful discussion.

Good afternoon to you all, dear delegates, our UN partners and development partners herein. In this session, we're going to take a deep dive into midwifery models of care used in Africa, their outcomes, their benefits, and possibly the transitioning strategies that countries have. I'm going to be your session lead for the last.
And my name is Dr. Jemima Araba-Denis-Entry. I am a midwife and a global public health professional. I'm also the founding president for the Center for Health Development and Research.

I'd like to give a little introduction into our session so that we can set the tone. And by so, I would like to say that midwifery models of care are models of care in which the main care providers for women and newborns, starting from the pre-pregnancy and continuing all the way through the postnatal period, is handled or provided by educated, licensed, regulated midwives who autonomously provide and coordinate respectful, high quality care across their full scope of practice using an approach that is aligned with the midwifery philosophy of care and which gives the opportunity to promote a person-centered approach to care, values the woman-midwife relationship and partnership, optimizes physical, biological, psychological, social, and cultural processes, and uses interventions only when indicated. Midwives in midwifery models of care provide integrated care addressing the needs of each individual woman and a newborn within functional and enabling health systems equipped with necessary resources and streamlined consultation and referral processes.

They collaborate within networks of care as part of interdisciplinary teams characterized by equity, trust, respect, and equality. This approach guarantees that every woman and newborn receive personalized care tailored to their health needs. On this panel, we hope to create the platform for a shared continental understanding and commitment to accelerating the adoption, adaptation, and scale-up of context-responsive midwifery models of care across African health systems.

Positioning midwives as autonomous, competent, and accountable primary providers of quality, respectful, continuous, and evidence-based care for women and their newborns within an interdisciplinary healthcare system. To do so, I proudly present to you my esteemed panelists right here with us. Within the West and Central Africa region, we have Dr. Eva Mensah from the Ministry of Health of Ghana.

Eva Mensah, can you come over, please? Can we put our hands together? Madam Bige Baimboji from the Senegal Midwives Association. Madam Jane Francis, Uganda Ministry of Health. From the Arab region, we have Dr. Jamar Egal, Somaliland Midwifery Association.

And to add spice, we have Madam Heather Gulliver of SEED Global Health, Malawi office to bring the NGO perspective to the discussion. Let's give them a big round of applause as we have this discussion. Thank you so much for agreeing to be part of this interesting discussion.

We all know that midwifery models of care is now an important narrative that we have been talking about in the past few years, looking at what the global direction is and the fact that we need to centralize or position the midwife in order to optimize maternal and newborn health. And therefore, we're going to have our final discussion looking at a number of issues to address for us. The focus of our discussion will be reviewing current MMOCs and the practical ways for the continent to transition to the midwifery models of care.
To set the ball rolling, I would like to start from Somaliland. Briefly describe the midwifery models of care that exist in your country. I give you two minutes, please.
Okay, is this on? Yes, okay. Hi, everyone. Thank you so much for listening to us and for the organizers of this amazing conference and gathering.

My name is Dr. Jama Igal and I'm the Associate Director or the Executive Director of the Somaliland Midwifery Association. In our context, we have a very well-working midwifery model of care in the sense of midwives are autonomous practitioners. They are autonomous within the community, but also in the health services and in the health facilities.
So they are the lead of midwifery services. They work within teams and groups. Education in midwifery is regulated.
We have different caters of midwives. Midwifery is a popular profession in Somaliland which helps. And midwives are in the community, in the rural areas, but also in the city.
So in that sense, we are on a head start from other settings. Thank you. Thank you very much for setting the tone, Somaliland.

Can we now have Ghana? Tell us what midwifery models of care do we have in Ghana? Okay, thank you very much, Dr. Nsinkwe and a good afternoon to us all. So in Ghana, we are working towards a 2030 goal of good health and wellbeing. And we are riding on universal health coverage.

And so with this universal health coverage, we've aligned it to get various levels of healthcare services. And so I'll start with the lowest level that we call the CHIPS. And with the CHIPS, it's a community level where we have placed midwives to work there.

And the midwives, the midwifery of maternal and child health services is midwife-led. And so they take care of the women, right from antenatal family planning services, to postnatal care services. What limits their work is setting guidelines and rules that prompt them when the condition of the mother or the child is above their level, then they are required to refer.
And so there are certain criteria that we have set in place so that they refer. From the community, which is the CHIPS level, we move to the health center. The health center is also midwifery-led.

And so midwives work at the health center. And so the referral is expected to come from the community to the health center. And when it's above the midwife at the health center, it's also midwife-led, as I said.

If it's above here, also we have the safe motherhood strategies, which also define what can be done at the health center. And so from there, it's referred to a district level hospital or polyclinic. The work of the midwife is collaborative.
So it's not necessarily midwifery-led in its entirety. There are other players within the field. But in that field as well, there is a referral to the regional level hospital.

The regional level hospital is also collaborative. And so it's not only the midwife, as I said, but then when it comes to normal labor, that one is managed by the midwife. So the midwife can do the ANC for a normal woman.

But when it's a high-risk mother, that's when an OB-GYN is the one who will manage. And same with tertiary-level hospitals too, because they are referred by an obstetrician-gynecologist from either a district level or a regional level. At the tertiary level, the OB-GYN will pick, because this is somebody who is coming with a challenge.

But then when it's seen as something that can be managed by a midwife, the OB-GYNs allow the midwives to handle it at the tertiary level. Yeah, thank you, thank you so much. For Uganda, there is not much difference.
And the midwifery models of care. My name is Jane Frances Acham, and I work at Minis Pro-Care. In Uganda, we recognize midwives as the, as the midwives who are in charge of the midwifery.

Primary, primary in midwifery work, in maternal and newborn services in the country. And we have the midwifery-led models of care, midwifery-led models of care in Uganda. And we have levels of care, that is the health center, two, three.

That is, those are the BMOC facilities where midwives primarily are the service caregivers. So majority of our mothers, they live in the BMOC facility, where midwives are primary caregivers. So that is the midwifery-led model of care.

And then when we move up the tertiary, the CMOC facilities from health center for to the National Faro Hospital, we have a collaborative model of care by the midwives and obstetricians, whereby the midwives handle the normal cases. And when the labor becomes complicated, they work hand-in-hand with the obstetricians. That is in the public setting.

But also we have the Private Midwives Association of Uganda. They also have midwifery-led bus centers that primarily the midwives are the ones who deliver the service. We also have the community model, where the midwives work with the village health teams and the community extension health workers to do integrated outreaches in the community so that they deliver the services.
So those are the models we have in Uganda. Thank you so much. Thank you so much for this insight.
Now, we will go to Senegal. Senegal, what models do you have? Thank you very much. In Senegal, we have experienced up to now five models.

In the beginning, we had what we call the binomials in each health post, that is, the lowest structure in the sanitary pyramid. Before, there was no midwife, there were only midwives. But then, when we had what we call the winning couple, the Minister of Health and the Government of Senegal asked what we are.
A midwife coupled with a midwife in each health post. We started that in 2014, and it continues to this day. Today, we are at 74 or 75% of health posts that are coupled.

So we find midwives everywhere, in the most primary level. These midwives are responsible and autonomous, and it is up to them to make all the decisions, whether to refer, whether to give birth, and so on. Then, there was a project called the itinerant midwives, that is, there were 50 midwives who had been recruited in two regions where there were the least number of midwives, because they were the most remote and the poorest regions.

So the midwives did not accept to stay in these areas. So the health posts did not have midwives. So the project recruited 50 midwives who were in the post, but who only did community activities, whether it was prenatal consultations, postnatal consultations, family planning, even childbirth, they could go directly to the communities and do it.

So that's a project that ended about ten years ago, which was evaluated, but unfortunately we could not continue because there was a problem of recruitment in Senegal. And so the third was the sound networks, because in the case of sound networks, we had to choose which maternities could be included in the sound network, that is, maternities where all the care is directed by midwives, but also with the possibility of having a gynecologist or a doctor, which we call sound doctors, that is, they are general practitioners who have been trained to do a caesarean. So every time the midwife gave the diagnosis, even if there was no gynecologist, there was a sound doctor who could do this caesarean.

So the sound network is based on how to ensure that within two hours a woman can be evacuated and have the necessary care to reduce maternal mortality. After that, there was the delegation of tasks, always in the case of sound networks, and that's how, for 20 years, midwives have been trained to do echography in all the regions of Senegal, in all the basic structures, new health posts, new health centers. And at the level of hospitals, it is true that it is the gynecologists who do the echographies, but the midwives also, so I myself am part of the training in obstetrical echography compared to midwives and in the case of sound.

And the last thing is that there is a community action, what we call the neighborhood midwives, in Wolof it is called the badjanugor, they are people who work with midwives, who have been trained to detect signs of danger and signs of emergency, which means that it is themselves who bring the women to the midwives, and every time a midwife notices that the person has not come, so it is themselves who speak at the level of the community and make sure that these people come so that there is continuity of care. Thank you. Good, good.
Thank you so much. We've heard from Somalia, we've heard from Ghana, Uganda, now we come to Seed Global Health in Malawi. Tell us also what you've been doing as part of midwifery models of care.

Thank you all very much. I feel, having heard these very inspiring stories of midwifery leadership, that possibly Malawi, with all due respect for my colleagues here, may still be in the neonatal period when it comes to midwifery autonomy. So currently in Malawi, there is only one midwifery-led ward.

A very brief story around that is, 2019 and 20, through commitment and leadership, through my dearest colleague, Dr. Usula Kapalufula, she was the lead driver for the establishment of a midwifery model of care in Malawi. This was to take place at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, the referral hospital for central Malawi. At that time, approximately 9,000 births a year.

It was decided to be a alongside model of midwifery care within the grounds of Queen Elizabeth. It was quite a nice facility, a nice area. However, as a consequence of high numbers of pregnant women, COVID positive, that facility, that area where the midwifery model was to be launched, was utilised to care for vulnerable women that were COVID positive.

But as we all know, midwives are flexible and they are determined. So following the establishment of a tripartite MOU, led by the Malawi Ministry of Health and Sanitation, in close collaboration with my direct implementation partner which is the Kamuzu University of Health Sciences in Malawi, myself in Seed Global Health, established, not myself, but sorry, Seed Global Health, established the first midwifery-led ward, this time in an urban health facility with approximately 1,200 births per year. So a significant pivot.

But since then, through committed efforts to build autonomous practice across the scope for those midwives, and based on respectful and responsive maternity care, through this partnership, this three-way partnership and close engagement with the community, there's now a very successful and the only midwifery-led ward in Malawi and due to popular demand, the birthing numbers there now have doubled, which brings its own challenges. There have been no maternal deaths reported for quite some years. Evidence is very, yes, it's very important.

And evidence is clear from pre and post-testing of student midwives. They value the experience of working with the midwives in the unit there. And as a consequence of this, the partnership model led by our ministry has now joined forces with a consortium and we are currently in the process of a very ambitious rollout of midwifery models of care to four other sites in Malawi.
And one of those is one of our busiest hospitals with over 22,000 births per year. Great, great. From little things, big things grow.

This is wonderful, this is wonderful. Now, Ghana and Uganda, you did have very elaborate levels of care that you described, right from the community level through to the tertiary level. I would like you to probe and find out if the midwife allowed her full scope of practice at all these level based on the ICM essential competencies.
Uganda, can you start for us? Yeah, thank you so much. A true midwifery models of care goes beyond having a midwife present at delivery. It requires a scope of practice, which Uganda has.

So the scope of practice gives a midwife a full responsibility in the entire sexual, reproductive and maternal child health from family planning through intrapartum care, antenatal care, newborn resuscitation and postnatal care. It's also anchored in a person-centered partnership where a woman builds trust with a known midwife or a small team of midwives. It also protects normal physiological and biological processes and avoiding unnecessary interventions.

This scope of practice also has a scope of where the birth companion is chosen by the mother and when complications occur, midwives coordinate smoothly with timely referral to the higher facility. Those are from the lower health facilities or if they are in the CMOC facility, they consult obstetricians and work together with obstetricians. So that is the scope of practice we have in Uganda.
Thank you. Can you add on? Yes, so it's similar. It's similar.

It's similar. I think we are currently establishing teleconsultation where the midwife, she's allowed her full scope of practice but a teleconsultation provides an avenue to ask questions from an OBGYN from another level of a facility. So currently some of the regions have WhatsApp groups.

So when she has a challenge, she just types into the WhatsApp groups and the obstetrician and other midwives all over the country who can, within the region I should say, who can immediately say, no, we've seen this, this one we think is this, kindly refer her to the next level or you can do it yourself. You can provide this kind of interventions and that should be okay. So we have that around.

So I would say when it comes to, up to the primary healthcare level, midwives may function to their full scope. It's only when you get to the regional level and tertiary level hospitals where those there are referrals. So they are coming there with challenges.
That is where you have an OBGYN there who steps in as a collaborator for the care of the woman. Thank you. And that is where you tend to see the multidisciplinary team in action.

This is great. Now, Somaliland, based on the existing midwifery models of care you have, what do you think, which of the models do you think has worked and which have not worked and why? I think to also follow up on the previous question, we have only one model and we've only known this module and what we do is try and work from this module into filling the gaps that are, some of them have not been apparent before. As you go, you learn.

And others have just come up because of changes that are happening currently in the health, in every health system. And I think one of them is, for example, although yes, midwives are autonomous, and we have started from a place where midwives were autonomous in the health facilities, so the regional and the referral hospital, still some women who are not referred through the community decide to go to the hospital, to the maternity ward, and they are met with midwives, and midwives are autonomous there and provide all the care. But for those, from those women, some develop problems and challenges, and then those, that's where the midwives are working in collaboration with obstetricians and the neonatal midwifes that are working there.

But still, they are leading the care, but they ask the questions needed, they consult with the doctors where needed. But more and more now, we see that because of medicalization of birth, medicalization of midwifery care, we are seeing that it's those midwives in the regional hospitals that are complaining the most about losing their scope of practice. Some aspects of the scope of practice are being lost to junior doctors who are there.

There's more doctors available, and all of a sudden, midwifery's a hot topic, and everybody wants to deliver this baby, and there's more medical students available in the hospital. So all of a sudden, you see that junior midwives, experienced midwives, are complaining, whereas junior midwives are just, that's normal for them. They have to hand over, they have to ask the doctor, can I admit this woman, or can I not? But the junior or the senior midwives always say, we need to do it all.
The doctors used to ask for help and support. And now, these younger midwives are doing something that is completely foreign to us. And I think also we have a challenge with guidelines.

Guidelines are vital. What we focus on is emergency guidelines, or PPH guidelines, and all of these things, but what we don't consider is the normality guidelines. So we need guidelines, pathways, midwifery pathways, which identifies who is doing what, so that doctors don't come in and chip in little by little on the midwifery scope of practice, and because a woman has developed infection or whatever, all of a sudden, oh no, it's them taking over, or PPH, for example.

And I think one of the things that we at Somaliland Association are trying to do is to establish training that is interprofessional. Midwives are trained separately to obstetricians and doctors, and that has created, so we have the BMOC and the CMOC, absolutely needs to change, because what it created is people who are training in different training and separated, so how can they work together when it's about a woman? There's a PPH happening, and everybody's just looking at, oh, call the doctor, and you know, there's no feel of emergency, nobody is actually, they know the theory, the doctor has to do this and have to call them, and we are working as a team, but there's no teamwork there, it's all on the midwife, and they get the blame for when something goes wrong, and nothing to support them, because there's no guidelines that say that the doctor should have done anything. Thank you, thank you, thank you for this insight, and these are really true lived experiences that our midwives report about on our day-to-day way.

Now, as we round up, we want to look at, now we have shared quite a number of models, ranging from the district, the community, right through to the tertiary level, we have the Somaliland model, where the midwife is in charge, and then we have systems where in Malawi, we are setting up the midwife-led model, and where now is gaining attention, and more women desire to have midwife-led care. As we look into the future, as we seek to promote more midwifery-led care, what type of model of midwifery care do you suppose that Africa should concentrate on, and how should we transition into this model? I'm going to give the chance for each one of you to answer this question in one minute. So I will start from Madame Biguet from Senegal.

I would like to start from you. So which model do you think that we should promote, and how should we transition? Thank you. The model that we propose so that it can be integrated and declined at each level for Africa is the same model of midwifery practice that is integrated into a network of care with the midwife as the main provider at each level, and a collaboration with obstetricians and pediatricians.

So you are saying that the midwife should be at the community level, where she's the primary caregiver. Thank you. Uganda, what model do you propose, and how should we transition? Yeah, thank you so much.

The midwifery models of care that I would recommend is the midwifery-led models of care where the midwife is at the center, but also seconded by the collaborative model, because in case of any complication, the midwife has to refer to the higher authority. But the primary model is the midwifery-led model of care, and the continuity of care for the midwife at all levels of care. That is what I would recommend.

Thank you. Thank you. Ghana? So for Ghana, I wouldn't say for Ghana specifically, but I mean, if you read the literature, and I think I saw a Cochrane review in 2024, the proposal was for us to look at a continuity of care model with a known midwife and a small team.

And although, I mean, this review looked at researches that were done, most of them were outside Africa. So it means that we need to also look at a context-appropriate one for Africa, because for Ghana, sometimes a woman will go for her and seek out care services at the community level, and then she goes to get it at a district-level hospital, then she comes back to the community for postnatal care. So it's distort the continuity of care, because at all these levels, people would have bits and pieces of their history.

So I think this is a good forum for us to sit down and look at the experiences in the different countries and see which one would best fit, which one can be contextualized for each country or for maybe a sub-region where the nuances are similar. Thank you. Thank you.

Okay, so a lot has been said. But I think what I would add is, in the Somaliland context, I'm, or we are working on the setting. So at the moment is the maternal child health centers, health posts, and then you have, everything else is regional hospital or referral hospital.
But what we forgot to do is to connect the midwives to the homes. In Somaliland, about 70% of women like to deliver at home. And in other contexts, that is such an amazing thing.

For example, example of Holland or the UK or Sweden, that's the aim is to get more women to deliver at home. And then I came to Somaliland and it's the opposite. We want to get all the women to health facilities all of a sudden.
And that doesn't work because we don't have the number of midwives. We don't have the women who are willing to come. They don't have the funding for transport.

You have the problems that are related to being in a high risk setting. So we're asking women who are normal, who could have received better care at home or in the community, closest to the community, to come to the health facilities. And that is something we'd like to change in Somaliland, at least to get.
And one problem is we do have outreach. It's the word outreach. So midwives have learned through INGOs and NGOs to get funding to go to the homes and then that outreach.
And then when funding stops, they stop. Thank you. While it's part of their mandate, it's part of the training that they receive to be at home and also to the schools, sorry to say.
Midwives should be giving young girls education on reproductive health. They should be working on menstrual health. They should be working.
There's so much scope that is missing and that we need to think about. Thank you. Thank you so much, Dr. Iga.
Now our final comment from Seed Global. Thank you. What model do you think we should be looking at in Africa and how should we transition? Oh, thank you.

I believe because of the complexity of Africa, I believe deeply that each of you are the specialists in your own communities. I don't feel that a prescriptive model is necessarily an approach to follow. However, I strongly believe and encourage everyone considering midwifery models of care in Africa, that they should consider four foundational pillars that are non-negotiable, awaiting all the other pillars that are required.

And the first is respectful and responsive maternity care at every encounter for every woman in all ways, everywhere. Number two, we should be promoting and protecting physiological labour and birth, but also we should be promoting and protecting the mother-baby dyad across the continuum. We want healthy, well-nourished mothers to be having babies.

The mother-baby dyad is not just about essential newborn care. Number three, more relevant to us in Malawi perhaps, but strengthen autonomous midwifery practice across the scope. And number four is to promote a partnership model.

And you know your own context, but try and dismantle or remodel care provision that is fragmented. And I believe strongly from lessons learnt that you need to consider an implementation plan. How do you go about doing that? And for me and for us, I believe we should as midwives, we should midwife our midwifery models and we should midwife the midwives within those models.

And what does that mean? That means to be bold and courageous and reflective. We need to question what we are doing and are we serving those women in your, or you are serving the women in your own communities? And only in this way will we remain holistically and intentionally focused on those women that you are serving. And secondly, for implementation, this is enabling the midwives, it's midwifing the midwives.
We don't give up and turn our back when the woman has had the baby. So with your midwifery model, please continue to support those midwives to remain resilient and committed. Thank you.

Thank you so so much. Can we put our hands together for such a wonderful panel? We would have loved to go on and on, but time is against us. And therefore I would like to say thank you so much to my panelists for this wonderful insight.

So we realize that in Africa, we do have midwifery models of care, ranging right from the community to the tertiary level. We have learned from our panelists that depending on the level of operation, there may be some compromise scope of practice because they have to compete with other healthcare professionals. But we also realize that beyond the community and the sub-district level, from the district level going on, they have to contend with the multidisciplinary approach to healthcare.

And I think that this is the right order. Now, what we need to look at is putting the midwife central to everything that is within his scope of practice and empowering her to give the best care as defined within the competencies, essential competencies that have been described as our global guidelines. So ladies and gentlemen, as Africa, we go forth, we need to document all these levels of care and begin within the country to look at contextually which of these models we can adopt.
But within it, the midwife must be the center of care for all of us. Thank you so much. We would have loved to take questions, but time is against us.
